title: Jobs: Pixar's power structure is inverted, CEO at the bottom
dek: Top creative talent and top graphics talent are both extremely scarce and can leave anytime, so Jobs says Pixar's management inverts itself to serve them—the CEO becomes the bottom.
why: A 1996 interview, unhurried pace and not particularly dense, but two segments on inverted-pyramid talent management and stock-based retention without contracts deserve close attention.
who: Founders and managers interested in startup talent management and the fusion of creative and technical teams, plus fans of Pixar and Disney animation history.
skip: Two segments on Disney collaboration and future distribution plans (around 3:00–5:00) have low information density and can be skipped.

points.h: What he bought was a dream, not a company
points.body: In 1985, Jobs met Ed Catmull, then leading Lucasfilm's computer division, who described his dream of making the first fully computer-animated feature film. Jobs said he bought that dream ‘both financially and spiritually’—not just financially, but as an act of faith. The bet took ten years to come true, becoming Toy Story, cinema's first fully computer-synthesized feature, and one of the most commercially successful animated films ever made.

points.h: Elite talent only goes to a handful of companies
points.body: Jobs says Pixar leads the industry because it attracts two extremely scarce categories of people simultaneously—the world's best animation talent (who normally go only to Disney, Pixar, perhaps DreamWorks) and the world's best computer graphics talent. Most studios lack the technical culture to attract the latter. Pixar spent ten years synthesizing Hollywood culture and Silicon Valley culture—these two ‘really different’ cultures—into a system where both groups work as peers with equal standing, nearly unmatched in the industry.

points.h: Contract work margins eroded, so Pixar stopped doing it
points.body: Jobs reviews the past business model of computer animation—most people in the field operated as labor of love, making money by taking on ads and title sequences, work-for-hire jobs. The problem: these businesses kept getting squeezed. Even if a Listerine ad sold more Listerine, Pixar captured none of that upside, only per-job fees. As more competitors entered, margins collapsed. This year Pixar quit advertising entirely, pulling 25 top talents from contract work to focus on projects where the company retains ownership.

points.h: The CEO serves at the bottom of the hierarchy
points.body: Jobs says that in both Silicon Valley and Pixar, elite talent is extremely scarce; if not treated well, they can find another job in ten minutes. So ‘the hierarchy of power inverts’—power structure flips, with the CEO actually at the bottom. He says he feels he's working for these people, because they're the ones doing brilliant work; management's job is to clear obstacles for them on the front lines.

points.h: Hire 125 elite employees in one year without lowering quality
points.body: Pixar expanded this year from about 175 people to about 300, with the greatest challenge being ‘not to lower the quality bar one iota’. Jobs says the company built a strong recruiting team, using some ‘competitive advantages’ he wouldn't disclose, ultimately hiring 125 employees he called A-plus—he holds this up as exemplary of what management should actually do.

points.h: Disney taught Pixar: edit the film before you animate it
points.body: Jobs explains the fundamental difference between animation and live-action: live-action directors can shoot 10 to 25 times as much material as the finished film and rebuild the film in the editing room; animation is too expensive—even shooting 10% more is unaffordable—so the film must be edited before actual production. This ‘edit-first, animate-second’ methodology is experience Disney developed over decades and cannot be bought; collaborating with Disney gave Pixar direct access to that accumulated knowledge, which they internalized while making Toy Story and later improved upon.

points.h: Hollywood locks talent down with contracts, Pixar uses stock options
points.body: Hollywood and Silicon Valley use two completely different methods to retain talent: Hollywood relies on the contract ‘stick’, Silicon Valley on stock options as ‘carrot’. Jobs says signing contracts easily deceives managers—if someone has five years left, they don't worry, only starting to court them again six months before expiration, then filing them away again after renewal. Pixar chose the Silicon Valley model: give everyone stock, align everyone's interests, so the company thinks every day about making Pixar better—so good no one wants to leave—rather than binding people with a contract.

points.h: Technology makes richer images, but cannot fix a bad story
points.body: Jobs mentions Disney's 1937 Snow White, which a few years ago was rereleased on video and sold 28 million copies, netting roughly $250 million—sixty years later, the story still works for new generations. He believes people will still watch Toy Story sixty years hence, not because of computer graphics but because of the story about friendship. He also points to another technology curve: ten years ago, the short film Luxo Jr. took about three hours per frame to render; today computers are a hundred times faster, yet Toy Story still takes about three hours per frame, because visual complexity grew a hundredfold too—but he says ‘no amount of technology can turn a bad story into a good story’, something John Lasseter taught him and Pixar's true creed.

terms.def: A playful mashup of Silicon Valley and Hollywood: SV companies using tech narratives to enter content business, raising money on stories instead of shipped products.

quotes.text: I met Ed Catmull who was running the computer division of Lucasfilm in 1985 and Ed showed me what they were doing and he shared with me his dream about making the first computer animated feature film.
So if Listerine sold more Listerine because of our commercials, we didn't make any more money for producing the commercials.
But my greatest joy is when we have people that are much better than I am at something so I can not forget about it, not worry about it and get on to something else where I can help.
So the strange thing happens, which is the sort of the hierarchy of power inverts. And the CEO is actually at the bottom.
Hollywood uses the stick, which is the contract, and Silicon Valley uses the carrot, which is the stock option.
And I think I know, I think everyone I know knows the story of Snow White.
I think the art of storytelling is very old. And no amount of technology can turn a bad story into a good story.
